questions.question: Define the national budget and name four sources of government revenue. What happens when expenditure exceeds revenue?
questions.expected_answer: The national budget is government's plan of expected revenue and intended expenditure for the financial year (1 April to 31 March), presented by the Minister of Finance in February and passed by Parliament. Sources: tax revenue collected by SARS; non-tax revenue such as fees, fines, interest and dividends from state-owned enterprises; borrowing through bonds and loans; grants and donations. When expenditure exceeds revenue there is a budget deficit, which government finances by borrowing, adding to government debt and future interest payments.

questions.question: Distinguish between direct and indirect taxes, with three examples of each. Calculate the income tax payable on a taxable income of R200 000 at 18% with a primary rebate of R17 235.
questions.expected_answer: A direct tax is levied on the income or wealth of a person or business and paid by that taxpayer, who cannot pass it on: personal income tax (PAYE), company income tax, dividends tax, capital gains tax, estate duty, donations tax. An indirect tax is levied on goods and services, paid to SARS by the seller or importer and passed on to the buyer in the price: VAT, excise duties (sin taxes), fuel levy, customs duties. Tax: 18% × R200 000 = R36 000; R36 000 − R17 235 = R18 765.

questions.question: Explain progressive, proportional and regressive taxes with an example of each. Why is VAT regarded as regressive, and how does government reduce this effect?
questions.expected_answer: Progressive: the percentage of income paid in tax rises as income rises, e.g. personal income tax (brackets from 18% to 45%, plus rebates). Proportional: the same percentage for all, e.g. company tax at 27%. Regressive: lower-income earners pay a larger percentage of their income, e.g. VAT. VAT has one rate, but poor households spend all their income on taxed goods while richer households save part of theirs, so VAT takes a larger share of a poor household's income. Government reduces this by zero-rating basic foods and paraffin, exempting public transport, and spending revenue on grants and free services.
